<title><![CDATA[Children bear brunt of NHS waiting times in England, report finds]]></title>
<link>http://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-101246.short?rss=1</link>
<description><![CDATA[Tens of thousands of young people in England have been waiting more than a year for an NHS appointment, a report warns.1While waiting times for most adult services are improving overall, the opposite is happening in children’s services, the Care Quality Commission’s (CQC) annual state of care report showed. This contrast was sharpest in waiting times for community health services.While the report found that the number of adults waiting more than a year for an appointment had reduced, the number of young people waiting more than a year increased by 129% in the two years to March 2026.Most of those waits were for community paediatric services, including diagnosis of neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism and ADHD. Just a few weeks ago a major government backed review found that the process for diagnosing ADHD and autism in England needed a “fundamental shift” to ensure that children receive timely support.2The CQC said...]]></description>

<title><![CDATA[Consultants’ strike: Senior doctors in England announce industrial action]]></title>
<link>http://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-101242.short?rss=1</link>
<description><![CDATA[Consultants in England will strike for two days in November after negotiations on pay and working conditions broke down, the BMA says.The NHS’s most senior hospital doctors plan to walk out from 7 am on 25 November to 6 59 am on 27 November.The BMA’s Consultants Committee has been locked in a dispute with the government since May 2025. <title><![CDATA[Financial incentives may have a role in driving care quality, but they must be meticulously designed]]></title>
<link>http://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-101226.short?rss=1</link>
<description><![CDATA[A notable feature of the government’s 10 year health plan for England, Fit for the Future, was its insistence that incentives and a pay-for-performance culture would drive better value and outcomes.123 The recent publication of the National Quality Board’s quality strategy4 reaffirms the role of incentives in driving change. The strategy is optimistic that, with careful design, incentives could help in achieving many of the 10 year plan’s objectives.4Some of the proposals in the strategy are radical, including “patient power payments” that—starting with gynaecology services—will allow patients to decide whether provider organisations are fully reimbursed for their care on the basis of their experience.14 The aim of tackling persistent failures to listen to women56 is surely right, as is the broader aim of creating mechanisms to stimulate and sustain improvement. <title><![CDATA[Trump’s aid cuts risk killing women around the world]]></title>
<link>http://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-101191.short?rss=1</link>
<description><![CDATA[“Women’s rights are human rights. Reproductive rights are human rights. Sexuality rights are human rights. We are seeing an erosion of the narrative around that.”Those are the words of JE Musoba Kitui, director of the Ipas Africa Alliance, a non-profit focused on advancing access to safe abortions and contraception, in reaction to the “hugely problematic” cuts to health aid. A huge proportion of the cuts are being made by the US, the biggest global health funder at the time.On 20 January 2025, President Donald Trump ordered a 90 day pause on US foreign development assistance. By March, his administration said it had cancelled more than 80% of USAID programmes. Other health specific initiatives, including the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and the World Health Organization (WHO), also experienced major funding losses and disruption. <item rdf:about="http://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-100785.short?rss=1">
<title><![CDATA[Advances in the management of renal cell carcinoma]]></title>
<link>http://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-100785.short?rss=1</link>
<description><![CDATA[AbstractRenal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common form of kidney cancer, with 435 000 patients newly diagnosed worldwide each year. In addition to morphology and histology, molecular subtyping has advanced the diagnostic classification of RCC. Contemporary diagnosis relies on cross sectional imaging in the form of computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging and selective biopsy. For localised disease, nephrectomy remains the standard of care, with partial nephrectomy being an option for smaller tumours. Ablation or stereotactic radiation is appropriate for selected patients. Adjuvant pembrolizumab provides improved disease-free and overall survival in high risk clear cell RCC. In metastatic disease, the introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitor based combinations has extended overall survival, providing a durable response in some patients. Despite these advances, primary and secondary resistance, along with the lack of predictive and prognostic biomarkers, remain a challenge.]]></description>
